topics.title: HCF and LCM from numbers written as products of prime factors

cards.front: Two numbers are written as products of their prime factors. How is the HCF built from the two lists?
cards.back: Take only the primes that appear in **both** lists, each to the **lower** power, and multiply them.

cards.front: Two numbers are written as products of their prime factors. How is the LCM built from the two lists?
cards.back: Take **every** prime that appears in either list, each to the **higher** power, and multiply them.

cards.front: $A = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5^2$ and $B = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5$. Write the HCF as a product of primes and as a number.
cards.back: $2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$
cards.hint: Shared primes only, lower power each time.

cards.front: $A = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5^2$ and $B = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5$. Write the LCM as a product of primes and as a number.
cards.hint: Every prime, higher power each time.

cards.front: Quick check on a pair of answers: how are HCF, LCM and the two original numbers linked?
cards.back: HCF $\times$ LCM $=$ the product of the two numbers. For 600 and 180: $60 \times 1800 = 108\,000 = 600 \times 180$.
cards.source: checking device, not on the formula sheet

cards.front: Trap: you multiply every prime from both lists, each at its highest power, and write the result on the HCF answer line. What has gone wrong?
cards.back: That is the LCM. Sense-check the size: the HCF is no bigger than the smaller number, the LCM is no smaller than the larger one. Examiners regularly see a three-figure LCM offered as an HCF.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M3 Q20(b), M4 Q5(b)

cards.front: Trap: burgers come in packs of 12 and buns in packs of 18. You work out the LCM as 36 and stop. Why is that not the answer?
cards.back: The LCM is the number of **items**, not the number of packs. Divide it by each pack size: $36 \div 12 = 3$ packs of burgers and $36 \div 18 = 2$ packs of buns.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M3 Q23, M4 Q9

cards.front: What does the instruction "write 540 as a product of its prime factors in index form" require on the answer line?
cards.back: $2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5$ — primes only, in ascending order, repeats written as powers. A factor tree alone is working, not an answer.

cards.front: From two prime factorisations, how do you build the HCF and how do you build the LCM?
cards.back: HCF: keep only the primes that appear in both, each at its lower power, and multiply. LCM: keep every prime that appears in either, each at its higher power, and multiply.

cards.front: What does 'highest common factor' mean in words?
cards.back: The largest number that divides exactly into both numbers. It is never larger than the smaller of the two.

cards.front: What does 'lowest common multiple' mean in words?
cards.back: The smallest number that both numbers divide into exactly. It is never smaller than the larger of the two.

cards.front: A question says 'as few as possible, none left over'. HCF or LCM?
cards.back: LCM. Sharing out or cutting into equal pieces is the HCF; repeating events meeting again, or buying matching quantities, is the LCM.

cards.front: $\text{HCF}(a,b) \times \text{LCM}(a,b) = $ ?
cards.back: $a \times b$. It is a quick check: once you have the HCF, the LCM is $a \times b$ divided by it.

cards.front: You found the lowest common multiple of the two pack sizes. What is the very next thing to do?
cards.back: Read the answer line again. If it asks for packs, boxes, strips or minutes, divide or convert; the common multiple on its own is usually not the answer.

cards.front: $A = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 7$ and $B = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5$. Write the HCF and the LCM in index form.
cards.back: $\text{HCF} = 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$; $\text{LCM} = 2^4 \times 3^3 \times 5 \times 7 = 15\,120$.

topics.title: Reverse percentages: finding the original quantity

cards.front: You have divided to find the original amount. What one-line check confirms it?
cards.back: Apply the change **forwards** to your answer: it must return the value you were given. For an 18% discount, $60 \times 0.82 = £49.20$, the price in the question.

cards.front: Which words in a question tell you it is a reverse percentage rather than an ordinary percentage change?
cards.back: "Original", "before the increase", "was", "pre-sale", "cost price", "a year ago" — the value you are **given** is the one after the change, and the unknown is the one before it.

cards.front: A house sold for £10 225 after its value fell by 18.2%. Find the value before the fall.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M3 Q18, M4 Q7 (most found 18.2% and subtracted)

cards.front: A bill is £1008 after a 12% increase. What was the bill before the increase?
A laptop costs £328 in an 18% off sale. What was the price before the sale?
A car is worth £14 070 after depreciating by 6.2% in one year. What was it worth a year ago?
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q30, M4 Q15

cards.front: Trap: a price is £328 after 18% off, so you work out 18% of 328 and subtract it. Why does this score zero?
cards.back: The 18% was taken off the **original**, not off £328, so 18% of the sale price is the wrong quantity. Divide instead: $328 \div 0.82$.
cards.source: examiner reports: the commonest zero-scoring start in every series

cards.front: Trap: for a fall of 18.2% you divide by 0.82 instead of 0.818. How much does that matter?
cards.back: It changes the answer: $10\,225 \div 0.818 = 12\,500$ but $10\,225 \div 0.82 = 12\,469.51$. Use the exact multiplier, to as many decimals as the rate has.

cards.front: A savings account paid 4% compound interest for 3 years and now holds £5624.32. How many divisions does the reversal need, and what was the deposit?
cards.back: One division per year, so divide by $1.04^3 = 1.124864$: $5624.32 \div 1.124864 = £5000$.

cards.front: A price rose by 10%, then by 15%, and is now £10 120. What was the original price?
cards.back: $10\,120 \div 1.15 = 8800$, then $8800 \div 1.10 = £8000$. Two changes need two separate reversals.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M3 Q24, M4 Q10 (most reversed only one change)

cards.front: A first-class ticket costs 24% more than a standard ticket. The difference in price is £20.64. Find both fares.
cards.back: The difference is the 24%, so $20.64 \div 0.24 = £86$ standard, and $86 + 20.64 = £106.64$ first class.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M3 Q22 (many found £86 then stopped)

cards.front: Sense-check: reversing a **decrease** should give an answer of what size, and reversing an **increase**?
cards.back: Reversing a decrease gives a **larger** number than the one you were given; reversing an increase gives a **smaller** one. If your answer goes the other way, the multiplier was used upside down.

cards.front: The three lines of a reverse percentage, in order.
cards.back: 1 Write the percentage the given value represents: (100 ± r)% = the value. 2 Divide by that percentage to reach 1%. 3 Multiply by 100. On a calculator the whole thing is one division by the multiplier.

cards.front: Multiplier for an increase of $r\%$, and for a decrease of $r\%$?
cards.back: Increase: $1 + \frac{r}{100}$. Decrease: $1 - \frac{r}{100}$. An increase sits above 1, a decrease below it.

cards.front: A price rose by 28% and you are told the new price. Is the new price 128% or 72% of the old one?
cards.back: 128%. An increase puts the value you are given above 100%; 72% would be a decrease of 28%.

cards.front: What does depreciated mean, and what does it do to the percentage in the first line?
cards.back: Depreciated means fallen in value, so it is a decrease: the value you are given is below 100%. A fall of 6.2% makes it 93.8%.

cards.front: An amount was multiplied by 1.35. What single operation returns the original amount?
cards.back: Divide by 1.35. Multiplying by 0.65 does not undo it: $1.35 \times 0.65 = 0.8775$.

cards.front: You have reversed the percentage and found the original. What is the next thing to do?
cards.back: Read the question again and name the quantity it asks for. It may want the saving, the difference, the profit or the later price, and the original is only the middle of the working.

cards.front: Percentage change $=$ ?
cards.back: $\dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100$. The change goes on top; the amount it started from goes underneath.

cards.front: A bill is £72 including VAT at 20%. What is the bill before VAT?
cards.back: £72 ÷ 1.2 = £60. Including VAT means the 20% has already been added, so the £72 is 120%.

cards.front: An account paid 5% in year one and 2% in year two, and now holds £5355. How do you find the opening deposit?
cards.back: Divide by each multiplier in turn: $5355 \div 1.02 = 5250$, then $5250 \div 1.05 = 5000$. Two changes need two divisions, and the rates are never added.

cards.front: You have written 1% = £2.80 in a reverse percentage. What is still owed?
cards.back: × 100. The answer line wants 100%, so the original is £280; stopping at 1% loses the final mark.

cards.front: A sale price of £68 after a reduction of 15% means £68 = ____% of the original price.
cards.back: 85%. The reduction leaves 100% − 15% = 85%, so £68 ÷ 0.85 = £80.

cards.front: Your calculator shows 4820.5 for a money answer. What goes on the answer line?
cards.back: £4820.50. Money is written with two decimal places, and a missing trailing zero costs the accuracy mark.

topics.title: Upper and lower bounds in addition and multiplication

cards.front: A measurement is given to a stated degree of accuracy. How far either side of it do the bounds lie?
cards.back: Half of the rounding unit each way. Nearest whole number: $\pm 0.5$. One decimal place: $\pm 0.05$. Nearest 10: $\pm 5$. Nearest 5: $\pm 2.5$.

cards.front: A length is 38 cm to the nearest centimetre. Write the error interval.
cards.back: $37.5 \leqslant L < 38.5$

cards.front: A mass is 50 kg to the nearest 5 kg. Write the error interval.
cards.back: $47.5 \leqslant m < 52.5$. Half of 5 is 2.5, not 5.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q13 (45 used instead of 47.5)

cards.front: Which bounds give the greatest sum, and which give the greatest product, of two measurements $a$ and $b$?
cards.back: Both use the two upper bounds: greatest sum $=$ UB$(a) +$ UB$(b)$; greatest product $=$ UB$(a) \times$ UB$(b)$. The least sum and least product use the two lower bounds.

cards.front: A rectangle measures 6.4 cm by 3.2 cm, each to 1 d.p. Find the upper bound of its area.
cards.back: $6.45 \times 3.25 = 20.9625$ cm$^2$. Leave the full value unless the question asks for rounding.

cards.front: Trap: you work out the area from 6.4 and 3.2, then add 0.05 to the answer to get the upper bound. Why is that wrong?
cards.back: Bounds belong to the **inputs**, not the output. Substitute the bounds first, then calculate. Rounding or adjusting the final answer loses the accuracy marks.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q17 (bounds applied after calculating)

cards.front: Trap: for 38 cm to the nearest cm you write the upper bound as 38.49 or 38.4999. What is the accepted upper bound?
cards.back: 38.5. The upper bound is the exact halfway value, written with a strict inequality: $L < 38.5$. Values such as 38.49 are not accepted.

cards.front: What is an error interval, and how is it written?
cards.back: The set of values a rounded measurement could really have, written as a double inequality between the lower and upper bounds, for example $2.35 \leqslant x < 2.45$ for 2.4 to 1 d.p.

cards.front: What is the half unit for each of these: nearest whole number, 1 decimal place, 2 decimal places, nearest 10, nearest 5?
cards.back: 0.5, 0.05, 0.005, 5 and 2.5. The half unit is always half of the rounding step.

cards.front: Why is the half unit for 'to the nearest 5' equal to 2.5?
cards.back: The interval of values that round to it has width 5 and is centred on the stated value, so it reaches 2.5 either side.

cards.front: For the greatest possible SUM or PRODUCT of positive measurements, which bounds do you use?
cards.back: All upper bounds together; for the least, all lower bounds together. Mixing an upper with a lower belongs to subtraction and division, which are M4.

cards.front: Where do the bounds go: on the measurements, or on the answer?
cards.back: On the measurements, before any calculation. Working out the answer first and then adding a half unit to it is the error examiners report most on this topic.

cards.front: The calculator shows 19.4925 for an upper bound. What do you write?
cards.back: 19.4925, in full, with the unit. A bound is never rounded unless the question tells you to; rounding it changes what is being claimed.

cards.front: A length is 12 cm to the nearest cm. Write the error interval.
cards.back: $11.5 \le L < 12.5$. The lower bound is included because 11.5 rounds up to 12; the upper bound is not, because 12.5 rounds up to 13.

cards.front: A rectangle is 9 cm by 4 cm, each to the nearest cm. Upper and lower bounds of the area?
cards.back: Upper $= 9.5 \times 4.5 = 42.75 \text{ cm}^2$; lower $= 8.5 \times 3.5 = 29.75 \text{ cm}^2$.

cards.front: Which bounds question belongs to M4, not M3?
cards.back: Anything where the quantities are subtracted or divided — a difference in lengths, a speed, a density from mass and volume. In M3 the calculation is an addition or a multiplication, so the bounds always pair like with like.

topics.title: Equations vs identities and expanding two linear expressions

cards.front: Examiner vocabulary: what is the difference between an equation and an identity?
cards.back: An **equation** is true only for particular values of the letter and can be solved, for example $3x + 1 = 10$. An **identity** is true for **every** value of the letter, for example $(x+2)^2 \equiv x^2 + 4x + 4$.

cards.front: What does the symbol $\equiv$ tell you, and where would you meet it?
cards.back: It marks an identity: the two sides are equal for all values of the letters. It replaces $=$ when a statement is being asserted for every value rather than solved.

cards.front: Expand $(a + b)^2$ and $(a - b)^2$. Are these on the Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$ and $(a-b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2$. Neither is on the sheet — both must be known, and the middle term is the one candidates drop.
cards.source: packs/maths/exam-true/formula-sheets.json (not listed on the Higher sheet)

cards.front: Expand and simplify $(2y + 3)(3y - 4)$.
Expand and simplify $(n - 4)(n + 2)$.
Trap: after expanding you have $m^2 + m^2$ and write $m^4$. What is the correct simplification?
cards.back: $2m^2$. Adding like terms adds the **coefficients** and leaves the power alone; powers are only added when terms are multiplied.

cards.front: Trap: a question asks for a quadratic **expression** for an area and you write $(x + 3)(4x - 1)$ on the answer line, or set it equal to zero. What is wanted?
cards.back: The expanded, simplified expression $4x^2 + 11x - 3$. An expression is not equal to anything and is not left as a product; only an equation gets "$= 0$".
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M3 Q25, Summer 2025 M4 Q5

cards.front: Trap: expanding $(3x + 2)(4x - 5)$ you write $12x$ as the first term. Why must it be $12x^2$?
cards.back: $3x \times 4x = 12x^2$: the two $x$ terms multiply to give $x^2$. Every product of two linear brackets starts with an $x^2$ term.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M3 Q25, November 2025 M3 Q27

cards.front: What does $\equiv$ mean, and how is an identity different from an equation?
cards.back: $\equiv$ means the two sides are equal for every value of the letter. An equation is true only for particular values and asks you to find them; an identity is a statement that two expressions are the same thing.
$a^2 + 2ab + b^2$ and $a^2 - 2ab + b^2$. The middle term comes from the two identical cells of the grid.

cards.front: How many products does expanding two brackets give, and what is always true of the first one?
cards.back: Four, one for each pair of terms. The first is the product of the two leading terms, so it is always the squared term: $3x \times 2x = 6x^2$.
$2m^2$. Adding like terms adds the coefficients and leaves the power alone; $m^4$ would be $m^2 \times m^2$.
Squaring a bracket means multiplying it by itself, which produces four products, not two. The two middle cells are both $5x$, giving the $10x$.

cards.front: A question asks for the 'quadratic expression' for an area. What must the answer look like?
cards.back: Expanded and simplified, starting with the $x^2$ term, and not set equal to anything. A product left in brackets, or an equation ending in $= 0$, loses the accuracy mark.

cards.front: Expand and simplify $(x + 9)(x - 4)$.
cards.back: $x^2 + 5x - 36$. The middle term is $-4x + 9x = 5x$ and the constant is $9 \times -4 = -36$.

cards.front: You have expanded correctly but you are not sure. What is the ten-second check?
cards.back: Put a value such as $x = 2$ into the original and into your answer. An identity holds for every value, so the two must agree; if they do not, the slip is in the expansion.

topics.title: Factorising quadratics of the form x² + bx + c

cards.front: Steps for factorising $x^2 + bx + c$ into two brackets.
cards.back: 1 Find two numbers whose **product is $c$** and whose **sum is $b$**. 2 Write $(x + \text{first})(x + \text{second})$. 3 Expand mentally to check the middle term.

cards.front: Factorise $x^2 + 7x + 12$.
Factorise $c^2 - 12c + 27$.
cards.back: $(c - 3)(c - 9)$ — and keep the letter $c$, not $x$.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q28, M4 Q13

cards.front: Factorise $x^2 + 2x - 15$.
What do the signs of $b$ and $c$ tell you about the signs inside the two brackets?
cards.back: $c$ positive: both signs match the sign of $b$ (both $+$ or both $-$). $c$ negative: one $+$ and one $-$, and the larger number takes the sign of $b$.

cards.front: Trap: the question is in $c$ or in $p$, and you answer in brackets written with $x$. What does that cost?
cards.back: A mark, even when the numbers are right. Factorise in the letter the question uses, and check the signs reproduce the middle term.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q28, M4 Q13

cards.front: Trap: "Factorise $x^2 - 5x - 14$" and you write $x = 7$ and $x = -2$. What has gone wrong?
cards.back: Factorising produces brackets, not solutions: $(x - 7)(x + 2)$. Only "solve" asks for values of $x$.

cards.front: You have factorised a quadratic. What one-line check confirms it before you move on?
cards.back: Multiply the two constants: they must give $c$. Add them: they must give $b$. For $(x-3)(x-9)$: $-3 \times -9 = 27$ and $-3 + (-9) = -12$.

cards.front: To factorise $x^2 + bx + c$, what two conditions must your pair of numbers satisfy?
cards.back: They multiply to $c$ and add to $b$. Both conditions at once — a pair that gives the right product but the wrong sum is no use.

cards.front: What do the signs of $b$ and $c$ tell you before you start searching?
cards.back: If $c$ is positive the two numbers share a sign, and that sign is the sign of $b$. If $c$ is negative they have opposite signs, and the larger number takes the sign of $b$.
keyWords: larger takes the sign of b

cards.front: Why is the letter in the brackets not always $x$?
cards.back: Because the question chooses the letter. A quadratic in $c$ factorises into brackets in $c$; switching to $x$ costs a mark even when the numbers are right.

cards.front: The command is 'Factorise fully'. What extra step does 'fully' demand?
cards.back: Take out any common numerical factor first, and leave it in front: $2x^2 + 10x - 48 = 2(x + 8)(x - 3)$. Stopping at $2(x^2 + 5x - 24)$, or hiding the 2 inside a bracket, both lose marks.

cards.front: 'Factorise $x^2 - x - 20$' — what must the answer NOT contain?
cards.back: An equals sign. Factorising produces a product, $(x - 5)(x + 4)$; setting it equal to zero or giving $x = 5$ and $x = -4$ answers a different question.

cards.front: How do you check a factorisation in five seconds?
cards.back: Multiply the brackets back mentally: the two middle products must give the $x$ term and the two constants must give $c$. A sign slip shows up immediately in the middle term.

cards.front: Factorise $x^2 - 13x + 40$.
Factorise $n^2 + 2n - 63$.
State the difference of two squares factorisation. Is it on the Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: $a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$. It is **not** on the sheet, so it must be known.
cards.source: packs/maths/exam-true/formula-sheets.json (not listed on the Higher sheet)

cards.front: Factorise $x^2 - 49$.
Factorise fully $3x^2 - 75$.
cards.back: $3(x + 5)(x - 5)$ — take the common factor 3 out first, then use the difference of two squares.

cards.front: Factorise $25 - w^2$.
cards.back: $(5 + w)(5 - w)$. Keep the terms in the order given: $(w+5)(w-5)$ expands to $w^2 - 25$, the negative of what was asked.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q20 (terms reversed)

cards.front: Trap: the expression is $25 - w^2$ and you write $(w + 5)(w - 5)$. Why is that not accepted?
cards.back: It expands to $w^2 - 25$, which is the negative of the expression. When the squared term is second, the constant comes first in both brackets: $(5+w)(5-w)$.

cards.front: Factorise $4x^2y^2 - 9$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q18 (three letters)

cards.front: Factorise fully $12a^3 - 27a$.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q22 (common factor 3a, then the difference of two squares)

cards.front: Factorise $\frac{x^2}{4} - 9$.
cards.back: $\left(\frac{x}{2} + 3\right)\left(\frac{x}{2} - 3\right)$ — a fractional coefficient is still a square, since $\frac{x^2}{4} = \left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q19 (most scored zero on the fractional case)

cards.front: Trap: can $x^2 + 49$ be factorised by the difference of two squares?
cards.back: No. The rule needs a **subtraction** of two squares. A sum of two squares does not factorise, so $x^2 + 49$ is already in its simplest form.

cards.front: What does the instruction "factorise fully" require beyond a first correct step?
cards.back: Keep going until nothing in the brackets factorises further: highest common factor first (number and letters), then check each bracket for a difference of two squares or a quadratic.

cards.front: Non-calculator: use the difference of two squares to work out $87^2 - 13^2$.
cards.hint: The rule works with numbers as well as letters.

cards.back: $(a + b)(a - b)$. One bracket has a plus and the other a minus, so the two middle terms cancel and no $x$ term survives.

cards.front: How do you factorise $36 - p^2$, and why is $(p + 6)(p - 6)$ not accepted?
cards.back: $(6 + p)(6 - p)$. The first term of the expression leads both brackets. $(p + 6)(p - 6)$ expands to $p^2 - 36$, which is the negative of what was asked.

cards.front: Before using the identity, what is the first thing to check?
cards.back: Whether there is a common factor. $5x^2 - 45$ is not a difference of two squares as written, but $5(x^2 - 9)$ is, and 'factorise fully' expects the 5 out in front.

cards.front: Is $25a^2$ a perfect square? What is its square root?
cards.back: Yes. $\sqrt{25a^2} = 5a$, because $5a \times 5a = 25a^2$. A term is a square when its coefficient is a square number and its index is even.

cards.front: Does $x^2 + 25$ factorise?
cards.back: No. The identity needs a **difference**; a sum of two squares has no factorisation with real numbers. Two terms and a plus sign means stop.

cards.front: Factorise $9m^2 - 64$.
Factorise $\dfrac{x^2}{4} - 9$.
cards.back: $\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + 3\right)\left(\dfrac{x}{2} - 3\right)$, or equivalently $\tfrac{1}{4}(x + 6)(x - 6)$. A fraction can be a perfect square.

cards.front: How does the identity help without a calculator?
cards.back: It turns two awkward squares into one easy product: $101^2 - 99^2 = (101 + 99)(101 - 99) = 200 \times 2 = 400$.

cards.front: Why does the difference of two squares have no middle term?
cards.back: Expanding $(a + b)(a - b)$ gives $a^2 - ab + ab - b^2$, and the two middle products are equal and opposite, so they cancel.

cards.front: $\dfrac{x^2 - 16}{x + 4}$ — what is the first move?
cards.back: Factorise the numerator to $(x + 4)(x - 4)$, then cancel the whole bracket $(x + 4)$, leaving $x - 4$. Never cancel the $x^2$ against the $x$: only whole factors cancel.

topics.title: Algebraic fractions with numerical denominators: simplifying and solving equations

cards.front: Adding or subtracting two algebraic fractions with **numerical** denominators: the steps.
cards.back: 1 Lowest common denominator. 2 Multiply each numerator by the factor its denominator needed, keeping the numerator in brackets. 3 Expand, applying a minus sign to every term inside. 4 Collect like terms over the single denominator.

cards.front: Simplify $\frac{4x+3}{10} + \frac{6x-5}{5}$.
cards.hint: Common denominator 10, so the second numerator doubles.
cards.source: the spec's own worked example M3-NA-08

cards.front: Simplify $\frac{3x+1}{4} - \frac{x-2}{6}$.
Trap: subtracting $\frac{x-2}{6}$ you write $\ldots - 2x - 4 \ldots$ after expanding. What is the rule for a subtracted numerator?
cards.back: Bracket it first, then change **every** sign inside: $-2(x-2) = -2x + 4$. Subtracting only the first term is the commonest cap on marks in this topic.

cards.front: An equation contains fractions with numerical denominators. What is the safest first line?
cards.back: Multiply **every term on both sides** by the lowest common denominator and write that line out in full. Then expand brackets and solve the linear equation that is left.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M3 Q19 (those who multiplied through succeeded)
the spec's own worked example M3-NA-10

cards.front: Solve $\frac{2x-1}{3} = 5$.
Trap: you multiply $\frac{x}{3}$ by 3 and write $\frac{3x}{3}$. What should multiplying by the denominator do?
cards.back: Cancel it: $3 \times \frac{x}{3} = x$. Multiply the fraction as a whole, not the numerator on top of the same denominator.

cards.front: Trap: you multiply the fraction and the term beside it by 3, but leave the other side of the equation alone. Why does the working collapse?
cards.back: Both sides must be multiplied by the same number, term by term. An incorrect first line earns nothing and blocks follow-through marks.

cards.front: Trap: you turn $\frac{2}{3}$ into 0.667 to make the equation easier. What does that cost?
cards.back: Accuracy marks. Decimal versions of thirds, sixths and sevenths are rounded values, so the final answer misses the exact one. Keep every fraction exact to the end.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M3 Q19 and M4 Q8

cards.front: To clear the fractions from an equation, multiply every term on both sides by ____.
cards.back: The lowest common multiple of the denominators (for denominators 10, 5 and 2 that is 10).

cards.front: The four moves for writing $\dfrac{ax+b}{p} \pm \dfrac{cx+d}{q}$ as a single fraction.
cards.back: 1 Lowest common denominator of $p$ and $q$. 2 Multiply each numerator by what its denominator was multiplied by, keeping it in a bracket. 3 Expand, changing every sign inside a subtracted bracket. 4 Collect like terms and check whether the fraction cancels.

cards.front: Why must a subtracted numerator stay in a bracket?
cards.back: Because the minus sign belongs to the whole numerator. Removing the bracket changes the sign of every term inside it, and forgetting the second term is the most reported loss on this topic.

cards.front: How do you start solving an equation with numerical denominators?
cards.back: Multiply **every** term on both sides by the lowest common denominator, and write that line down. The fractions disappear and an ordinary linear equation is left.

cards.front: $\dfrac{x}{5} + 2 = 7$. What do the 2 and the 7 become when you multiply by 5?
cards.back: 10 and 35. Every term, on both sides, takes the multiplier — not only the fraction.

cards.front: Why not turn the fractions into decimals?
cards.back: Because one third is $0.333\ldots$, so decimals force a rounding at the first line and the accuracy marks go with it. Keeping the fractions exact is both safer and quicker.

cards.front: $\dfrac{2x + 1}{3} = 5$. What is the correct first line?
cards.back: $2x + 1 = 15$. Multiplying both sides by 3 cancels the denominator; multiplying the numerator by 3 as well would be doing it twice.

cards.front: $\dfrac{a}{p} + \dfrac{b}{q} = $ ?
cards.back: $\dfrac{aq + bp}{pq}$ — and if $p$ and $q$ share a factor, the lowest common denominator is smaller than $pq$ and keeps the numbers down.

cards.front: How do you check a solution to a fractional equation?
cards.back: Substitute it back into the original equation and evaluate both sides. It takes ten seconds and catches sign slips that re-reading will not.

cards.front: 'A number is increased by 5 and the result halved.' Write that in symbols.
cards.back: $\dfrac{n + 5}{2}$, with the whole of $n + 5$ over the 2. $\dfrac{n}{2} + 5$ is a different instruction.

cards.front: Which fractional equations are NOT part of this topic?
cards.back: Any with the unknown in a denominator, such as $\dfrac{2}{x+1}$: those are M4, and they clear to a quadratic. Here the denominators are always numbers and the equation stays linear.

cards.front: Write $\dfrac{2x + 7}{5} + \dfrac{x - 3}{2}$ as a single fraction.

topics.title: Simplifying, multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions (factorise and cancel)

cards.front: Simplifying an algebraic fraction: the steps.
cards.back: 1 Factorise the numerator fully. 2 Factorise the denominator fully. 3 Cancel only **whole brackets** that appear top and bottom. 4 Write what is left as a single fraction.

cards.front: Trap: in $\frac{x^2+5}{x^2+3x}$ you cancel the $x^2$ from top and bottom. Why is that not allowed?
cards.back: Only **factors** cancel, and $x^2$ is a term here, not a factor. Factorise first: the denominator is $x(x+3)$, the numerator has no factor in common, so nothing cancels.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M4 Q19 (single terms cancelled across the fraction)

cards.front: Simplify $\frac{x^2-9}{x^2+7x+12}$.
Simplify $\frac{2x^2-18}{x^2-x-6}$.
cards.hint: Common factor 2 first, then a difference of two squares.

cards.front: Trap: the numerator is $2x^2 - 18$ and you divide it by 2 to get $x^2 - 9$. What is the difference between that and factorising?
cards.back: Dividing changes the expression; factorising keeps it equal: $2x^2 - 18 = 2(x^2-9)$. The 2 stays in the answer unless it cancels with the denominator.

cards.front: Dividing one algebraic fraction by another: the steps.
cards.back: 1 Invert the **second** fraction and change $\div$ to $\times$. 2 Factorise every numerator and denominator. 3 Cancel whole brackets across the multiplication. 4 Leave one simplified fraction.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q22 (one in twenty finished)

cards.front: Work out $\frac{x+2}{6} \div \frac{x+2}{3}$.
Work out $\frac{x^2-4}{3x} \times \frac{9x^2}{x+2}$.
Factorise $3x + 3y + ax + ay$ by grouping.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q20 (grouping in the numerator troubled the less able)

cards.front: Factorising by grouping: how do you know you have done it correctly?
cards.back: After taking a factor out of each pair, the **same bracket** must appear in both parts. If it does not, re-pair the terms or change the sign taken out.

cards.front: Trap: faced with $\frac{x^2-9}{x^2+7x+12}$ you set it equal to zero and solve for $x$. Why is that wrong?
cards.back: "Simplify" asks for an equivalent expression, not a value. An expression has no equals sign, so there is nothing to solve.

cards.front: Which three factorising techniques should you check for before cancelling an algebraic fraction?
cards.back: Highest common factor, difference of two squares, and a quadratic in two brackets (including grouping for four terms). A hard question usually needs two of the three.

cards.front: What must be true before anything in an algebraic fraction can be cancelled?
cards.back: Both the top and the bottom must be written as products. Only a whole common factor cancels; a term inside a sum never does.

cards.front: Why can you not cancel the $x^2$ in $\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 7x + 12}$?
cards.back: Because $x^2$ is one term of a sum, not a factor of the whole expression. Compare with numbers: $\dfrac{2+3}{2+4}$ is $\dfrac{5}{6}$, not $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

cards.front: $\dfrac{a}{b} \times \dfrac{c}{d} = $ ? and $\dfrac{a}{b} \div \dfrac{c}{d} = $ ?
cards.back: $\dfrac{ac}{bd}$, and $\dfrac{a}{b} \times \dfrac{d}{c}$ — it is the **second** fraction that is turned over.

cards.front: The four steps for dividing algebraic fractions.
cards.back: 1 Flip the second fraction and multiply. 2 Factorise every top and every bottom. 3 Cancel whole brackets. 4 Write the single fraction that is left.

cards.front: Which factorising tools do you need on this topic?
cards.back: A common factor, the difference of two squares, a quadratic $x^2 + bx + c$, and grouping when there are four terms.

cards.front: $\dfrac{6x^2}{8x}$ — what happens to the letters?
cards.back: $\dfrac{x^2}{x} = x$: dividing powers of the same letter subtracts the indices. The numbers cancel separately, so the answer is $\dfrac{3x}{4}$.

cards.front: You have simplified an algebraic fraction. What must the answer NOT contain?
cards.back: An equals sign, and no value of $x$. 'Simplify' asks for a tidier expression; solving is a different question.

cards.front: $(5 - w)$ and $(w - 5)$ — how are they related, and how do you use it?
cards.back: $(5 - w) = -(w - 5)$. Pull the $-1$ out so the two brackets match, cancel them, and leave the minus sign in front of the fraction.

cards.front: Simplify $\dfrac{2x + 10}{x^2 - 25}$.
Simplify $\dfrac{ab + 3a + 2b + 6}{b^2 - 9}$.
cards.back: Group the top: $a(b + 3) + 2(b + 3) = (a + 2)(b + 3)$. The bottom is $(b + 3)(b - 3)$, so the answer is $\dfrac{a + 2}{b - 3}$.

cards.front: Which algebraic-fraction questions belong to M4, not here?
cards.back: Adding or subtracting fractions whose denominators contain the unknown, such as $\dfrac{2}{x+2} + \dfrac{3}{2x-1}$. This statement covers simplifying, multiplying and dividing only.

topics.title: Setting up and solving quadratic equations by factorising

cards.front: Solving a quadratic equation by factorising: the steps.
cards.back: 1 Rearrange to $= 0$ with the terms in order. 2 Factorise into two brackets. 3 Set **each** bracket equal to zero. 4 Write both solutions on the answer line.

cards.front: Solve $x^2 = 5x + 24$.
Solve $4a^2 - 36 = 0$ by factorising.

cards.back: $x = 7$ or $x = -2$ — a product is zero only when one of its factors is zero.

cards.front: Trap: you factorise correctly and write only the positive solution. What does that cost?
cards.back: The final accuracy mark. Two brackets give two solutions, and both go on the answer line unless the question's context rules one out.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M4 Q10, Summer 2025 M4 Q10(b)

cards.front: Trap: to solve $x^2 - 4x = 12$ you subtract $x^2$ and divide by $-4$. Why does this fail?
cards.back: A quadratic cannot be unwound like a linear equation because the unknown appears twice. Collect everything on one side and factorise (or use the formula in M4).

cards.front: Trap: you spot that $x = 5$ works by trying numbers and write it down. Why is that risky?
cards.back: Trial finds at most one root and earns no method marks. The scheme rewards the factorised line, which produces both roots.

cards.front: Setting up a quadratic from a worded or geometric problem: the steps.
cards.back: 1 Name the unknown and write each length or quantity in terms of it. 2 Write the fact (area, Pythagoras, total) in words, then in algebra with every expression bracketed. 3 Expand and collect to $= 0$. 4 Solve, then check which root fits the context.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M3 Q28 (only a handful set up the equation)

cards.front: A rectangle is $x$ cm by $(x+3)$ cm and its area is 40 cm². Form an equation and find $x$.
cards.back: $x(x+3) = 40 \Rightarrow x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0 \Rightarrow (x+8)(x-5) = 0$, so $x = 5$ ($x = -8$ is rejected: a length cannot be negative).

cards.front: When may you leave one root out of a final answer, and what must you write?
cards.back: Only when the context forbids it — a negative length, time or count. State both roots first, then the reason for rejecting one, for example "$x = -8$ rejected as a length must be positive".

cards.front: The four steps for solving a quadratic by factorising.
cards.back: 1 Rearrange so that one side is zero. 2 Factorise. 3 Set each bracket equal to zero. 4 Give both solutions.

cards.front: Why does setting each bracket to zero work?
cards.back: Because a product can only be zero when one of its factors is zero. If neither bracket were zero, their product would be some non-zero number.

cards.front: You have $(x + 8)(x - 3) = 0$. What are the solutions?
cards.back: $x = -8$ and $x = 3$. Each bracket is solved, not copied: $x + 8 = 0$ gives $-8$.

cards.front: Why must you never divide both sides of $x^2 = 6x$ by $x$?
cards.back: Because it assumes $x$ is not zero, and $x = 0$ is one of the solutions. Rearrange to $x^2 - 6x = 0$ and factorise to $x(x - 6) = 0$ instead.

cards.front: A context question gives the roots 5 and −8. What do you write?
cards.back: The value the context allows, with a reason for rejecting the other: 'a length cannot be negative, so $x = 5$'. Silently dropping a root does not earn the mark.

cards.front: 'Hence solve' follows a 'Factorise' part. What does it mean?
cards.back: Use the factorisation you have just written. Another method, including trial or the formula, is not the route the scheme rewards here.

cards.front: What must a 'Show that' answer do?
cards.back: Start from the information given and reach the printed line, with every step visible. Substituting the answer in, or starting from the printed line, earns nothing.

cards.front: How do you set up a quadratic from a rectangle with a given diagonal?
cards.back: The diagonal and the two sides form a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras gives $a^2 + b^2 = d^2$. Expand any squared bracket in full, collect, and take everything to one side.

cards.front: $(31 - x)^2$ — what is the expansion?
cards.back: $961 - 62x + x^2$. Squaring a bracket means multiplying it by itself, so there is always a middle term.

cards.front: Solve $x^2 + 4x = 12$.
Which quadratics are NOT solved by this method?
cards.back: Any that will not factorise over the integers, and any where the coefficient of $x^2$ is not 1 and has no common factor. Those need the quadratic formula, which is M4.

topics.title: Straight lines: y = mx + c, finding the equation of a line, parallel lines

cards.front: In $y = mx + c$, what do $m$ and $c$ stand for, and is the form given on the Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: $m$ is the gradient and $c$ is the $y$-intercept (the $y$ value where the line crosses the $y$-axis). It is not on the sheet, so it must be known.

cards.front: State the gradient formula for a line through $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$.
cards.back: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ — the change in $y$ on top of the change in $x$.
keyWords: change in y over change in x

cards.front: Finding the equation of a line through two given points: the steps.
cards.back: 1 Gradient $m = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$. 2 Substitute $m$ and **one** of the points into $y = mx + c$. 3 Solve for $c$. 4 Write the equation as $y = mx + c$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M3 Q16 (only the top candidates finished)

cards.front: Find the equation of the line through $(2, 5)$ and $(6, 17)$.
Find the equation of the line through $(-1, 9)$ and $(3, 1)$.
cards.hint: Downhill from left to right, so expect a negative gradient.

cards.front: Trap: asked for "the equation of the line through the two points", you work out $\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$. What have you found?
cards.back: The midpoint — a point, not an equation. The answer must be of the form $y = mx + c$.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M3 Q22 and November 2025 M3 Q31

cards.front: Trap: you calculate $\frac{x_2-x_1}{y_2-y_1}$ for the gradient. What does that give?
cards.back: The reciprocal of the gradient. Gradient is always change in $y$ **over** change in $x$; check the sign against the direction of the line as well.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q2, November 2025 M4 Q16

cards.front: One of the two given points is $(0, 8)$. What does that tell you immediately?
cards.back: $c = 8$, because the point lies on the $y$-axis. Only the gradient still has to be found, and no substitution is needed.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q16 (few noticed c could be read off)

cards.front: What is true about the gradients of two parallel lines, and how do you write the equation of a line parallel to $y = 4x - 3$ through $(2, 11)$?
cards.back: Parallel lines have **equal** gradients. So $m = 4$, and $11 = 4(2) + c$ gives $c = 3$: $y = 4x + 3$.

cards.front: Find the gradient and $y$-intercept of $3x + 4y = 20$.
cards.back: $4y = -3x + 20$, so $y = -\frac{3}{4}x + 5$: gradient $-0.75$, intercept 5. Always rearrange to $y = mx + c$ before reading $m$.

cards.front: Trap: on a real-life graph you count squares between two points and write the gradient as 1.5. What must you use instead?
cards.back: The coordinate **values** read with the axis scales, not square counts. Choose two points far apart that sit on grid intersections, then divide the change in the vertical quantity by the change in the horizontal one.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M3 Q14 and M4 Q2

cards.front: A cost graph for hiring a machine has gradient 35 and intercept 20, with cost in pounds against days. Interpret both numbers.
cards.back: The gradient is the cost per day, £35 per day; the intercept is the fixed charge of £20 paid before any days are counted.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q2 (interpretation needed 'cost per day')

cards.front: In $y = mx + c$, what are $m$ and $c$?
cards.back: $m$ is the gradient — how much $y$ rises for each 1 that $x$ increases. $c$ is the $y$-intercept, the $y$ value where the line crosses the $y$-axis.
$m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ — change in $y$ on top. Take both differences with the points in the same order.
keyWords: change in y over change in x

cards.front: The three steps for finding the equation of a line through two points.
cards.back: 1 Find $m$ from the gradient formula. 2 Substitute either point into $y = mx + c$ and solve for $c$. 3 Write the whole equation $y = mx + c$.

cards.front: A question asks for 'the equation of the line'. What is the commonest wrong answer?
cards.back: The midpoint. An equation is a rule beginning $y =$; a midpoint is a single point. Read the answer line before you start.

cards.front: One of the two points has $x = 0$. What does that save you?
cards.back: The whole substitution: that point is on the $y$-axis, so its $y$ value **is** $c$. Only the gradient still has to be worked out.

cards.front: What is the gradient of $3y = 12x + 5$?
cards.back: 4. Divide every term by 3 first: $y = 4x + \tfrac{5}{3}$. No gradient can be read until $y$ is on its own.

cards.front: What is true of two parallel lines?
cards.back: They have equal gradients and different $y$-intercepts. Same $m$, different $c$ — so they never meet.

cards.front: How do you find the line parallel to a given line through a given point?
cards.back: Take the gradient of the given line (rearranging first if necessary), write $y = mx + c$ with that $m$, substitute the point and solve for $c$.

cards.front: Why must you not count squares to find a gradient on a real-life graph?
cards.back: Because the two axes usually go up in different steps. Read the actual values at two points and divide the change in the vertical quantity by the change in the horizontal one.

cards.front: How do you interpret a gradient on a real-life graph?
cards.back: In the units of both axes: 'the cost rises by £12 for each extra day'. A bare number, or scatter-graph language about correlation, does not earn the mark.

cards.front: How do you find where $3x + 4y = 24$ crosses each axis?
cards.back: Put $x = 0$ for the $y$-intercept, giving $(0, 6)$; put $y = 0$ for the $x$-intercept, giving $(8, 0)$. Those two points are also the quickest way to draw the line.

topics.title: Tangent, arc, sector, segment; arc length and sector area

cards.front: The shaded shape has radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ at the centre. Write the formula for the length of the marked arc.
cards.back: Arc length $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$. It is **not** on the Higher formula sheet, so it must be known.

cards.front: Write the formula for the area of a sector of radius $r$ with angle $\theta$ at the centre. Is it given to you?
cards.back: Sector area $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$. Not on the Higher sheet — recall it, together with $A = \pi r^2$ for the whole circle.

cards.front: The diagram names three parts of a circle. State in words what each of a tangent, a chord and a segment actually is.
cards.back: A **tangent** is a straight line touching the circle at one point, at right angles to the radius there. A **chord** is a straight line joining two points on the circle. A **segment** is the region between a chord and the arc it cuts off.

cards.front: A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 100°. Find the arc length to 1 d.p.
cards.back: $\frac{100}{360} \times 2\pi \times 9 = 15.7$ cm

cards.front: A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 100°. Find its area to 1 d.p.
cards.back: $\frac{100}{360} \times \pi \times 9^2 = 70.7$ cm²

cards.front: What does the **perimeter** of a sector consist of, and what is it for the 9 cm, 100° sector?
cards.back: The arc plus the two radii: $15.7 + 9 + 9 = 33.7$ cm. A perimeter includes every edge, straight ones too.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M3 Q20 (most halved the circumference and stopped)

cards.front: Find the perimeter of a semicircle of radius 6 cm to 1 d.p.
cards.back: Half the circumference plus the diameter: $\pi \times 6 + 12 = 30.8$ cm
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M4 Q5 (the diameter was not added)

cards.front: Trap: the diagram marks an angle of 40° but the arc drawn is the long way round. Which angle do you use?
cards.back: $360 - 40 = 320$°. Check which arc is drawn: a **major** arc uses the reflex angle, and only the minor arc uses the marked angle.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q12 (the majority gave the minor arc 6.1 cm instead of the major arc 15.9 cm)

cards.front: Trap: for a 260° arc you work out the circumference and then divide it by 260. What is the correct operation?
cards.back: Multiply by $\frac{260}{360}$. The fraction of the circle is the angle **over 360**, so an arc of more than half the circle must come out bigger than half the circumference.

cards.front: Trap: the question asks for the perimeter of a shape made of an arc and two straight edges, and you use $\pi r^2$ somewhere. How do you tell area from length?
cards.back: A length has one dimension: only $2\pi r$ and straight edges may appear, and the answer is in cm. Anything with $r^2$ is an area, in cm².
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M7 Paper 1 Q12, Summer 2025 M3 Q26

cards.front: Trap: you use 3.14 for $\pi$ on a calculator paper, or round the arc length part way through. What do examiners expect?
cards.back: The calculator's $\pi$ key and the full display carried to the end, rounding only on the final line to the accuracy asked for. An answer "in terms of $\pi$" keeps $\pi$ in it instead, for example $12\pi$ cm.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M7 Paper 1 Q12 (3.14 used)

cards.front: A sector of radius 12 cm has an arc of length 20 cm. Find the angle at the centre to 1 d.p.
cards.back: $\theta = \dfrac{20}{2\pi \times 12} \times 360 = 95.5$°
cards.hint: The arc is that fraction of the whole circumference.

cards.front: What is the formula for the length of an arc?
cards.back: Arc = (θ/360) × 2πr, where θ is the angle at the centre. It is a fraction of the circumference.

cards.front: What is the formula for the area of a sector?
cards.back: Sector area = (θ/360) × πr². It is the same fraction of the circle, applied to the area.

cards.front: Are arc length and sector area on the CCEA Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: No. Neither is printed, and neither is the circumference or the area of a circle. All four have to be known.

cards.front: How do you find the perimeter of a sector?
cards.back: Find the arc, then add both radii. Perimeter = arc + 2r.

cards.front: The angle marked at the centre is 100° but the arc drawn is the long way round. Which angle do you use?
cards.back: 260°, because the major arc uses 360 − 100. Check the diagram before substituting; the two arcs add to the circumference.

cards.front: Define a tangent to a circle.
cards.back: A straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point. The CCEA Teacher Guidance for M3-GM-01 uses that wording.

cards.front: What is the difference between a sector and a segment?
cards.back: A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc, like a slice of pizza. A segment is bounded by a chord and an arc, the piece cut off by a straight line across the circle.

cards.front: How do you find the perimeter of a semicircle?
cards.back: Half the circumference plus the diameter: πr + 2r, or (πd/2) + d. The straight edge is part of the outline.

cards.front: A sector answer comes out in cm². What must the question have been asking for?
cards.back: An area, not a length. An arc length or a perimeter is in cm; only the sector area is in cm².

cards.front: A sector of radius 15 cm has an angle of 24°. Give the arc length in terms of π.
cards.back: 2π cm. The fraction 24/360 is 1/15, and 1/15 of 30π is 2π.

cards.front: You know the arc length and the angle. How do you find the radius?
cards.back: Write arc = (θ/360) × 2πr as an equation, then divide by the fraction and by 2π: r = arc × 360 ÷ (θ × 2π).

topics.title: Surface area and volume of cylinders, cones and spheres (and hemispheres)

cards.front: Which four cone and sphere formulae are printed on the Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: Volume of a sphere $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$; surface area of a sphere $4\pi r^2$; volume of a cone $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$; curved surface area of a cone $\pi r l$.

cards.front: Give the volume, curved surface area and total surface area of a cylinder. Are they on the sheet?
cards.back: $V = \pi r^2 h$, curved $S = 2\pi r h$, total $S = 2\pi r h + 2\pi r^2$. None of them is on the sheet — all must be known.

cards.front: The sheet gives $\pi r l$ for a cone. What is the **total** surface area of a solid cone, and what is $l$?
cards.back: Total $= \pi r l + \pi r^2$ — the curved surface plus the base circle, which the sheet does not give. $l$ is the slant height, found by $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$.

cards.front: Write the volume and the two surface areas of a hemisphere of radius $r$.
cards.back: $V = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$ (half the sphere). Curved surface $= 2\pi r^2$; a solid hemisphere with its flat face showing has total surface $2\pi r^2 + \pi r^2 = 3\pi r^2$.

cards.front: A cylinder has radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Find its volume to 1 d.p.
cards.back: $\pi \times 5^2 \times 12 = 942.5$ cm³

cards.front: A cone has radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find its curved surface area to 1 d.p.
cards.back: $l = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13$, so curved surface $= \pi \times 5 \times 13 = 204.2$ cm²
cards.hint: The sheet gives pi r l, not pi r h.

cards.front: A sphere has radius 6 cm. Find its volume and surface area to 1 d.p.
cards.back: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi \times 6^3 = 904.8$ cm³; $S = 4\pi \times 6^2 = 452.4$ cm²

cards.front: Trap: the question is about the paper label wrapped round a tin, and you reach for $\pi r^2 h$. How do you decide between volume and surface area?
cards.back: Anything you wrap, paint or cover is a **surface area** (cm²); anything you fill or pour is a **volume** (cm³). A label is the curved surface only: $2\pi r h$.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M3 Q24, Summer 2025 M3 Q19

cards.front: A label wraps round a tin of height 12 cm and overlaps itself by 1 cm. How is the overlap handled?
cards.back: The overlap is extra **length** around the tin: label area $= (2\pi r + 1) \times 12$, or work out $2\pi r h$ and add the rectangle $1 \times 12 = 12$ cm². Adding 1 to the area or to the radius is wrong.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q13, M3 Q24 (few fully correct)

cards.front: Trap: a container is a cylinder with a hemisphere on top, filled to 90%, and the question asks how many 50 ml cups it fills. Which three slips do examiners see?
cards.back: Using a whole sphere instead of half; forgetting the 90%; and rounding the number of cups up. A count of full cups always rounds **down**.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M3 Q24, M4 Q9 (round down to 16 cups)

cards.front: A sector of card is rolled into a cone. What are the two links between the sector and the cone?
cards.back: The sector's arc length becomes the **circumference of the cone's base**, and the sector's radius becomes the cone's **slant height**. Equating those gives the sector angle.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q23 (rare to make the correct link)

cards.front: Trap: a question asks you to prove two surface areas can never be equal and you try $r = 1$, then $r = 2$. Why does that earn nothing?
cards.back: Examples cannot prove "never". Set the two expressions equal, divide through by $r^2$, and show the remaining constants differ — the argument stays in letters.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q20 (7% full marks)

cards.front: Trap: the diagram gives a diameter of 12 cm and you substitute 12 into the formula. What is the first line to write?
cards.back: $r = 6$. Every circle formula uses the **radius**, so halve any diameter before it goes near $\pi r^2$, $\pi r l$ or $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q6 (r = 12 used for a diameter of 12)

cards.front: Which solid formulae are printed on the CCEA Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: Volume of a cone (1/3)πr²h, curved surface area of a cone πrl, volume of a sphere (4/3)πr³, surface area of a sphere 4πr², volume of a prism and area of a trapezium. Nothing for the cylinder.

cards.front: Give the volume and the total surface area of a cylinder.
cards.back: V = πr²h and S = 2πrh + 2πr². Neither is on the formula sheet.

cards.front: Give the volume and the curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius r.
cards.back: Volume = (2/3)πr³ (half the sphere) and curved surface = 2πr². A solid hemisphere also has a flat circle of πr².

cards.front: A cone's volume and its curved surface area need different lengths. Which is which?
cards.back: Volume uses the perpendicular height h; πrl uses the slant height l. They are linked by l² = r² + h².

cards.front: A question asks for the total surface area of a solid cone. What do you add to πrl?
cards.back: The base circle, πr². The formula sheet gives the curved surface only.

cards.front: How many cubic centimetres are in a litre?
cards.back: 1000 cm³, the volume of a cube of side 10 cm. To change cm³ to litres, divide by 1000.

cards.front: You divide a container's volume by a cup's volume and get 16.4. How many full cups?
cards.back: 16. A count of full cups is rounded down, whatever the usual rounding rule would say.

cards.front: A cylinder's volume and radius are given. How do you find the height?
cards.back: Divide the volume by the area of the circular cross-section: h = V ÷ πr².

cards.front: A question gives you a volume. What does that usually mean?
cards.back: That the volume is the start of the working, not the finish: you are being asked for something you have not found yet, such as a height, a radius or a number of containers.

cards.front: A sphere of radius 3 cm is melted and recast as a cylinder of radius 2 cm. What is the cylinder's height?
cards.back: 9 cm. The sphere is 36π cm³, the cylinder's cross-section is 4π cm², and 36π ÷ 4π = 9.

cards.front: What does curved surface area mean for a cylinder, and what does total surface area add?
cards.back: Curved surface area is the tube alone, 2πrh, the rectangle you get by unrolling it. Total surface area adds the two circular ends, 2πr².

cards.front: State the pressure formula and the two rearrangements. Is it on the Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$, so $F = P \times A$ and $A = \dfrac{F}{P}$. Compound measures are not on the sheet and must be known.

cards.front: Which units go with pressure, and what does 1 pascal mean?
cards.back: Force in newtons over area in square metres gives N/m², called the pascal (Pa); 1 Pa is 1 N spread over 1 m². With areas in cm² the unit is N/cm².

cards.front: A box exerts a force of 560 N on a floor through a base of area 0.25 m². Find the pressure.
A block exerts a pressure of 40 N/m² over a contact area of 2.5 m². Find the force.
Trap: a cube of side 5 cm presses on a table and you divide the force by 125 or by 150. Which number should you divide by?
cards.back: 25 — the area of the **one face in contact**, $5 \times 5$. 125 is the volume and 150 is the total surface area, and neither touches the table.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q25, M4 Q10

cards.front: What single line should you write before using $P = F/A$ in an exam?
cards.back: "Area in contact $= \ldots$", naming the face. Examiners diagnose the loss of marks as focus on the formula rather than on which surface is actually touching.

cards.front: A solid with a square base exerts a force of 560 N and a pressure of 2240 N/m². Find the length of one edge of the base.
cards.back: $A = 560 \div 2240 = 0.25$ m², so the edge is $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$ m.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q25 (candidates divided the area by 4)

cards.front: Trap: you have found the base area of a square and divide it by 4 to get the edge. What should you do?
cards.back: Take the **square root**: a square of area $A$ has side $\sqrt{A}$. Dividing by 4 is the perimeter idea, not the area one.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q25, M4 Q10

cards.front: Two solids of different shapes press on the floor with the same pressure. What equation does that give you?
cards.back: $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$ — write each pressure as force over the area in contact, set them equal, and solve for the unknown area or force.

cards.front: Write the pressure formula, and its two rearrangements.
cards.back: Pressure = force ÷ area; force = pressure × area; area = force ÷ pressure.

cards.front: Which area goes into the pressure formula?
cards.back: The area in contact with the surface — the face that is actually touching. Not the total surface area, and never the volume.

cards.front: What is a pascal?
cards.back: One newton per square metre. 1 Pa = 1 N/m², so a pressure in N/m² is already in pascals.

cards.front: How many square centimetres are in a square metre?
cards.back: 10 000, because a square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm. To change cm² to m², divide by 10 000.

cards.front: A square base has area 64 cm². How do you find its side, and why not divide by 4?
cards.back: Take the square root: √64 = 8 cm, because side × side gives the area. Dividing by 4 is what you would do to a perimeter.

cards.front: Two objects exert the same pressure. How do you find an unknown base area?
cards.back: Work out the pressure from the object you know everything about, then use area = force ÷ pressure on the other one.

cards.front: A question asks for the force from a pressure, just after a part that asked for a volume. What must you not do?
cards.back: Do not feed the volume into the pressure formula. Go back for the area in contact; the reports note that many candidates reuse the previous answer instead.

topics.title: Trigonometry (sin, cos, tan) in right-angled triangles; angles of elevation and depression

cards.front: The triangle is labelled from the angle $\theta$. Say what decides each of the three names, and what happens to the labels if the other acute angle is marked instead.
cards.back: The **hypotenuse** is always opposite the right angle (the longest side). The **opposite** is the side facing $\theta$. The **adjacent** lies between $\theta$ and the right angle. Move to the other acute angle and the opposite and adjacent swap; the hypotenuse never moves.

cards.front: Write the three trigonometric ratios. Are they on the Higher formula sheet?
cards.back: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{O}{H}$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{A}{H}$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{O}{A}$. They are not on the sheet — SOH CAH TOA must be recalled.

cards.front: The steps for finding a missing side with trigonometry.
cards.back: 1 Mark the angle and label H, O, A. 2 Tick the side you know and the side you want. 3 Choose the ratio containing both. 4 **Rearrange first**, then substitute. 5 Round only at the end, to the accuracy asked.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q24 (cos identified but not rearranged)

cards.front: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 12 cm and the angle at the base is 35°. Find the adjacent side to 2 d.p.
The side opposite a 40° angle is 7 cm. Find the hypotenuse to 1 d.p.
cards.back: $\sin 40° = \dfrac{7}{h}$, so $h = \dfrac{7}{\sin 40°} = 10.9$ cm
cards.hint: When the unknown is on the bottom, it swaps with the ratio.

cards.front: A right-angled triangle has opposite 5 cm and adjacent 8 cm. Find the angle to 1 d.p.
Define the angle of elevation and the angle of depression.
cards.back: Both are measured from the **horizontal**: elevation is the angle you look **up** through, depression the angle you look **down** through. The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom (alternate angles).

cards.front: Trap: two sides are given and the question asks for an angle, so you use Pythagoras. What is needed instead?
cards.back: An inverse ratio: $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$ or $\tan^{-1}$ of the fraction the two sides make. Pythagoras only ever produces a third **side**.

cards.front: Trap: an isosceles triangle has base 1.4 m and you use 1.4 in a ratio. What must you do first?
cards.back: Drop the perpendicular from the apex to make two right-angled triangles and use **half** the base, 0.7 m. SOH CAH TOA needs a right angle.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q8 (weaker candidates used the full 1.4 m)

cards.front: Trap: the kite is 34.6 m above the holder's hand and the holder is 85 cm tall, so you write 34.6 + 85. What is the correct total height?
cards.back: $34.6 + 0.85 = 35.45$ m. Convert to a common unit before adding, and check the unit the answer is wanted in.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M4 Q12, M3 Q23

cards.front: Trap: in a two-triangle problem you round the shared side to 1 d.p. before using it again. What does that cost?
cards.back: The accuracy mark. Store the unrounded value (or use the calculator's answer key) and round only the final answer.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2025 M4 Q16, Summer 2023 M3 Q23

cards.front: How should you set out a chain of two or three triangles?
cards.back: Take one triangle at a time: write which triangle you are in, which ratio you are using and what it gives, then carry that unrounded length or angle into the next triangle.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q14 (40% full marks)

cards.front: Trap: your calculator gives 41.409622 for an angle and you write 41.4 when the question said 1 decimal place, but earlier you wrote 41 for a length in metres. What is the rule?
cards.back: Give exactly the accuracy the question asks for, on the final line only. If none is stated, 1 d.p. for angles and 3 significant figures for lengths are safe.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q21 (forgot to round to 1 d.p.)

cards.front: Write out SOH CAH TOA in full.
cards.back: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse; cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse; tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.

cards.front: How do you label a right-angled triangle before choosing a ratio?
cards.back: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Then, from the angle you are using, the side facing it is the opposite and the side beside it is the adjacent.

cards.front: Is SOH CAH TOA on the CCEA formula sheet?
cards.back: No. The sheet gives the sine rule, the cosine rule and (1/2)ab sin C, which are for triangles without a right angle. The three ratios must be known.

cards.front: cos 40° = 12 ÷ h. How do you find h?
cards.back: Multiply both sides by h, then divide by cos 40°: h = 12 ÷ cos 40°. When the unknown is underneath, the final step is a division.

cards.front: Two sides are known and you want the angle. What do you do?
cards.back: Write the ratio those two sides give, then apply the inverse: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹. The ratio on its own is not the angle.

cards.front: What is an angle of elevation, and what is an angle of depression?
cards.back: Both are measured from the horizontal. Elevation is the angle you look up through; depression is the angle you look down through.

cards.front: An angle of depression from a cliff top: which angle in the triangle is it equal to?
cards.back: The angle of elevation from the object at the bottom, because the two horizontal lines are parallel and these are alternate angles.

cards.front: Why must you not round a side before using it in a second triangle?
cards.back: The error carries into the next calculation and moves the final answer, which costs the accuracy mark. Keep the full calculator value and round once at the end.

cards.front: An isosceles triangle has no right angle. How do you use trigonometry on it?
cards.back: Drop a perpendicular from the apex to the base. That makes two right-angled triangles, each with half the base, and it gives half the angle at the apex, so double it at the end.

cards.front: A height in centimetres has to be added to a length in metres. What comes first?
cards.back: Convert: divide the centimetres by 100. Adding without converting is a wrong answer the examiners have traced more than once.

cards.front: A ladder 4.6 m long leans at 71° to the ground. How far is its foot from the wall?
cards.back: 1.5 m. The ground is adjacent to the angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so the distance is 4.6 × cos 71° = 1.4977 m.

topics.title: Quartiles and interquartile range from a list

cards.front: For $n$ ordered values, where do the lower quartile, median and upper quartile sit?
cards.back: At positions $\frac{1}{4}(n+1)$, $\frac{1}{2}(n+1)$ and $\frac{3}{4}(n+1)$ in the ordered list. Order the data first — the positions are meaningless otherwise.

cards.front: What does the interquartile range measure, and how is it calculated?
cards.back: The spread of the **middle 50%** of the data: IQR $=$ upper quartile $-$ lower quartile. Because it ignores the top and bottom quarters, one extreme value does not change it.

cards.front: Find the median, quartiles and IQR of 4, 5, 7, 8, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20.
cards.back: $n = 11$: median is the 6th value, 10; LQ is the 3rd, 7; UQ is the 9th, 15; IQR $= 15 - 7 = 8$.

cards.front: Find the median, quartiles and IQR of 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 14, 20.
cards.hint: A quarter of the way between the 2nd and 3rd values.

cards.front: What is an outlier, and what does it do to the range and the IQR?
cards.back: A value lying far outside the pattern of the rest of the data. It stretches the **range**, which uses the extremes, but leaves the **IQR** almost untouched, which is why the IQR is the fairer measure of spread when one is present.

cards.front: Trap: you find the quartile positions and write 3 and 9 as the answers. What has gone wrong?
cards.back: Those are **positions**, not values. Count to that place in the ordered list and give the data value found there.

cards.front: Trap: the axis or the table says "salary (£1000s)" and you give the IQR as 12. What is missing?
cards.back: The scale: the IQR is £12 000. Read the units of the axis or column heading before writing any statistic down.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M3 Q24(c), M4 Q11(c)

cards.front: Trap: the list reads 12, 3, 15, 8, 7 and you take the median as 15. What is the first step with any list?
cards.back: Put it in order: 3, 7, 8, 12, 15, so the median is 8. Every quartile rule assumes an ordered list.

cards.front: When is the IQR a better measure of spread than the range, and how should you say so?
cards.back: When the data contains an extreme value. Name it: "the range is inflated by the single value of 98%, so the IQR describes the spread of most of the data better."
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M3 Q26(b) (generic answers scored nothing)

cards.front: Where is the lower quartile of an ordered list of n values?
cards.back: At position ¼(n + 1).

cards.front: Where is the upper quartile of an ordered list of n values?
cards.back: At position ¾(n + 1).

cards.front: interquartile range = ?
cards.back: upper quartile − lower quartile

cards.front: What must be done to a list of values before any quartile is found?
cards.back: Put the values in order, smallest to largest.

cards.front: A quartile position works out as 3.5. What value do you write down?
cards.back: The value halfway between the 3rd and 4th values of the ordered list, that is, their mean.

cards.front: What does a small interquartile range tell you about a data set?
cards.back: The middle half of the values are close together, so the data is more consistent.

cards.front: Why is the interquartile range often preferred to the range?
cards.back: The range is fixed by the two extreme values, so a single unusual value can stretch it; the interquartile range uses only the middle half.

cards.front: The lower quartile is 14 and the interquartile range is 9. What is the upper quartile?
cards.back: 23, because UQ = LQ + IQR.

topics.title: Cumulative frequency tables and curves; estimating median, quartiles and IQR

cards.front: What does a cumulative frequency value mean, and how is the column built?
cards.back: The running total of the frequencies: how many values are **less than or equal to** the upper boundary of that class. Add each frequency to the total so far; the last entry equals $n$.

cards.front: At which $x$ value is each cumulative frequency plotted?
cards.back: At the **upper class boundary**, never the midpoint or the lower boundary. For $20 < t \leqslant 30$ the point is at $t = 30$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M3 Q24 (plots split between upper, mid and lower bounds)

cards.front: The curve is drawn for 60 values and the dashed lines show the construction. Which axis is $\frac{n}{2}$ measured on, what are the three steps, and roughly what median does this curve give?
cards.back: Start at $\frac{n}{2} = 30$ on the **vertical** (cumulative frequency) axis, read across to the curve, then straight down to the horizontal axis: about 26 minutes here.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M3 Q26 (median read as 12.5 on the horizontal axis)

cards.front: For 60 values, at which cumulative frequencies do you read the lower quartile and the upper quartile?
cards.back: $\frac{n}{4} = 15$ for the LQ and $\frac{3n}{4} = 45$ for the UQ, both read on the vertical axis. The IQR is the difference of the two horizontal readings.

cards.front: Trap: with 60 values whose times run from 0 to 50 minutes, you give the median as 25 minutes. Which axis has been halved by mistake?
cards.back: The horizontal one. The median comes from halving the **frequency** (30 on the vertical axis), not from halving the range of the measurement.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M3 Q26 (median given as 12.5)

cards.front: Trap: you plot the cumulative frequencies as a bar chart, or join the points with a ruler. What is expected?
cards.back: Points at the upper boundaries joined by a **smooth curve** (a straight-line polygon is usually condoned; bars score nothing and lose all follow-through marks).
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M4 Q13 (a bar chart scored nothing)

cards.front: A curve for 80 values gives readings LQ 22 s, median 31 s, UQ 46 s. State the IQR.
How do you estimate how many values lie **between** two given measurements from the curve?
cards.back: Read the cumulative frequency above each value and subtract: (reading at the larger) $-$ (reading at the smaller).
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M3 Q27 (only the best read both and subtracted)

cards.front: 60 people are timed. The curve reads 46 at 35 minutes. How many took **more** than 35 minutes?
cards.back: $60 - 46 = 14$ people. A cumulative reading is always "how many so far", so subtract from the total for "more than".

cards.front: Trap: the reading you need falls between two grid lines and you round it to the nearest line. What do examiners expect?
cards.back: A committed reading between the lines, judged against the scale. Mark schemes allow a tolerance, but a reading forced onto a grid line often falls outside it.

cards.front: Trap: the horizontal axis reads "salary (£1000s)" and you write the IQR as 12. What is the answer?
cards.back: £12 000. Convert every reading into the units of the axis before comparing or writing an answer.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2025 M3 Q24(c), M4 Q11(c)

cards.front: Why is a median found from a cumulative frequency curve only an **estimate**?
cards.back: The data has been grouped, so the individual values are unknown; the curve assumes the values spread evenly through each class.

cards.front: What is a cumulative frequency?
cards.back: The running total of the frequencies up to and including that class.

cards.front: At which value of the variable is each cumulative frequency plotted?
cards.back: At the upper class boundary.

cards.front: Why is the class midpoint the wrong place to plot a cumulative frequency?
cards.back: The running total is only complete once the whole class has been counted, which happens at the top of the class.

cards.front: How do you estimate the median from a cumulative frequency curve?
cards.back: Read across from n ÷ 2 on the cumulative frequency axis to the curve, then straight down to the variable axis.

cards.front: Which cumulative frequencies do you read across from for the two quartiles?
cards.back: n ÷ 4 for the lower quartile and 3n ÷ 4 for the upper quartile.

cards.front: How do you estimate how many values are greater than a given value?
cards.back: Read the cumulative frequency at that value, then subtract it from the total.

cards.front: How do you estimate how many values lie between two given values?
cards.back: Read the cumulative frequency at each value and subtract the smaller reading from the larger one.

cards.front: A reading falls between two grid lines. What do you write?
cards.back: The value you actually read; examiners expect readings that are not on grid lines.

cards.front: The horizontal axis is marked in £1000s and the interquartile range reads 12. What is the answer in pounds?
cards.back: £12 000, because each unit on the axis is £1000.

cards.front: What happens if you draw a bar chart instead of a cumulative frequency curve?
cards.back: The drawing scores nothing, and any part that reads from the graph loses its follow-through marks too.

cards.front: A cumulative frequency graph is drawn for 140 values. At what heights do you read the median and the two quartiles?
cards.back: 70 for the median, 35 for the lower quartile and 105 for the upper quartile.

topics.title: Box plots, comparing distributions and inferring from samples

cards.front: Read the box plot: state the median, the interquartile range and the range of the marks.
cards.back: Median 25; IQR $= 35 - 20 = 15$; range $= 45 - 10 = 35$. The box gives the quartiles, the whisker ends give the extremes.
